glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
anderkilla-shahi-jame-mosque.desc: Persian inscriptions date this mosque to 1667, when Shaista Khan was governor of Bengal, just after the Mughals took Chattogram from the Arakanese. It stands on a raised hill called Ander-Qila, the 'inner fort', which gave the whole neighbourhood its name. In 1761 the British used it to store arms, and it was only returned for prayer in 1855 after local Muslims petitioned. It is still one of the city's best-known mosques, and in 2025 the government decided to restore it.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or CNG to Anderkilla in old Chattogram, a short ride from Jamalkhan, Laldighi or the court hill.
Good to know
Non-Muslim visitors should come outside prayer times and ask before entering. Dress modestly. Laldighi and the court hill (Pori Pahar) are close by for a walk.

kala-bhuna.desc: Kala bhuna means 'black fry', and the name describes it well. Chunks of beef are cooked slowly with onions, garlic, ginger and a heavy hand of whole spices, then fried in their own fat until the pieces turn dark and dry at the edges. The result is intense and slightly smoky. It is a point of pride in Chattogram and a fixture at weddings and celebrations.

khoiyachora-waterfall.desc: Khoiyachora falls in several tiers down a forested gully in Mirsharai, north of the city. The walk in follows a shallow stream over stones and through bamboo and scrub, which is half the fun. The lowest tier is easy to reach, while the upper steps need careful climbing. It runs strongest during and just after the monsoon.
blocks: How to get there
Take a highway bus to Boro Takia bazar in Mirsharai, then a CNG to the trail start; the walk takes about an hour each way.
Good to know
Wear shoes with grip, avoid the upper tiers after heavy rain, and go with a local guide if you are unsure of the trail.

guliakhali-sea-beach.desc: Guliakhali is unlike a typical sandy beach. At low tide the ground is a carpet of short green grass cut by small tidal channels, with mangrove saplings planted along the edge of the sea. It feels open and quiet, especially on weekdays, and the light at sunset turns the water channels silver. It combines easily with a morning hike up Chandranath.
blocks: How to get there
From Sitakunda bazar take a CNG for about 20–30 minutes to the beach.
Good to know
Check tide times; the grassland is best at low tide. Wear sandals you can get muddy.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
chittagong-war-cemetery.desc: The Chittagong War Cemetery is maintained by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and holds the graves of servicemen who died on the Burma front during the Second World War. Rows of identical headstones lie on neat lawns under tall trees, close to the city centre. The graves include British, Indian, African, Japanese and other soldiers. It is a quiet green corner in a busy city.
blocks: How to get there
Rickshaw or CNG to Badshah Mia Chowdhury Road near Chawkbazar/Panchlaish in Chattogram city.
Good to know
Visiting hours are limited; go in the morning or afternoon on a weekday. Keep voices low.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
chandranath-hill-sitakunda.desc: Chandranath is one of the most important Hindu pilgrimage sites in Bangladesh, and the temple on its summit draws huge crowds during the Shiva Chaturdashi festival. For travellers it is also a rewarding hike: a long staircase and dirt trail climb through the Sitakunda hills, passing smaller shrines on the way. From the top you can see the coastal plain stretching to the sea on one side and forested ridges on the other.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus on the Dhaka–Chattogram highway to Sitakunda bazar (about 1 hr from the city), then a short rickshaw or CNG ride to the trailhead.
Good to know
Start early and carry water. The steps get slippery in the rain. Dress modestly and remove shoes at the temple.

glance: Shutki shops at Asadganj, Chattogram city; local rice hotels in the city serve shutki bhuna and bhorta
chattogram-shutki-asadganj.desc: Shutki, sun-dried sea fish, is part of almost every Chittagonian home kitchen. Loitta and churi shutki are cooked into fiery bhunas and bhortas with plenty of garlic and chilli, and the dishes have moved from home kitchens onto restaurant menus. Asadganj near the Karnaphuli, which locals call the shutki bondor, is the old wholesale hub where you can see and buy many kinds of dried fish.

jabbarer-boli-khela.desc: This traditional wrestling competition was started in 1909 by a local merchant, Abdul Jabbar Saudagar, partly to build strength and spirit among young Bengalis under British rule. It is held each year on the 12th of Boishakh (late April) at Laldighi Maidan. Wrestlers, called boli, grapple in a sand ring while crowds cheer, and the streets around fill with a multi-day fair selling handicrafts, household goods and snacks.

glance: winter (Dec–Jan), spring (Feb–Mar), summer (Apr–May), monsoon (Jun–Jul), autumn (Aug–Sep) and late autumn (Oct–Nov)
ethnological-museum-chattogram.desc: Set up in 1965 and opened to the public in 1974, this small museum in Agrabad is the only one of its kind in the country. Its galleries show the dress, tools, weapons, ornaments and household things of the hill and plains peoples of Bangladesh, with dioramas of daily life. More rooms were added between 1985 and 1995, and a gallery of folk objects from Bengali village life came in 1996. It is a quick, quiet stop that helps a lot before a trip to the Chittagong Hill Tracts.
blocks: How to get there
CNG or bus to Agrabad; the museum is on Sabdar Ali Road near Badamtali roundabout.
Good to know
Pair it with a visit to the hill districts; it makes the cultures you meet there easier to understand. Check the weekly closing day before going.

glance: Traditional Chittagonian restaurants in Chattogram city, and at wedding feasts across the district
chattogram-durus-kura.desc: Kura is the Chittagonian word for chicken, and durus means the bird is cooked whole. The chicken is skinned, rubbed with ginger-garlic and onion paste and garam masala, then fried and simmered until tender in a thick gravy; some cooks tuck boiled eggs in with it. Families in greater Chattogram have long served it to a new groom or bride and to honoured guests, usually with polao or khichuri.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
napittachora-trail.desc: Napittachora is a forest stream in Khoiyachora union of Mirsharai, inside the Baraiyadhala hills. Walking up the rocky stream bed from Nayduar, trekkers reach a series of falls and pools, including Kupikatakhum, Mithachori and Bandarkhum. The trail takes a few hours and is most rewarding in the rainy season when the falls are full. It sees far fewer visitors than nearby Khoiyachora.
blocks: How to get there
Take a Dhaka-bound bus from Chattogram to Nayduar (Mirsharai) on the highway, then walk east to the trailhead; local guides are available.
Good to know
Go with a group or a local guide; people have been injured on this trail. Wear grippy sandals and avoid it during heavy rain.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
patenga-sea-beach.desc: Patenga lies at the southern tip of the city, close to the airport and the river mouth. The shore here is lined with concrete blocks rather than open sand, but the view is the draw: cargo ships waiting to enter the port, fishing boats, and planes coming in low overhead. In the evening families gather for fried crab, sea fish and spiced tea from the stalls along the promenade.
blocks: How to get there
About 45 minutes by CNG or ride-share from central Chattogram, depending on traffic.
Good to know
Sunset is the best time. Swimming is not safe here because of strong currents and shipping traffic.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
parki-beach.desc: Parki Beach lies in Anwara, across the Karnaphuli River from Chattogram city, where the river meets the Bay of Bengal. It is a long, flat stretch of sand backed by rows of casuarina (jhau) trees. From the shore you can watch the cargo ships waiting at the outer anchorage of Chattogram port. It is much less crowded than Patenga, and at sunset the beach is calm and open.
blocks: How to get there
From Chattogram city cross the Karnaphuli (by the Shah Amanat Bridge or the Karnaphuli tunnel) toward Anwara, then take a CNG to Parki; about 1–1.5 hours.
Good to know
Do not swim far out; there are no lifeguards and currents near the river mouth can be strong. Carry water and snacks; facilities are basic.

foys-lake.desc: Foy's Lake was created in the 1920s by damming a hill stream, mainly to supply water to the railway colony nearby. Today it is a privately run leisure park, with boats gliding along narrow arms of the lake between steep wooded hills. There is an amusement park and resort on site, but the quieter corners of the water are the real reason to come.
blocks: How to get there
Located in the Khulshi/Pahartali area, a short CNG or ride-share trip from GEC Circle.
Good to know
Ticket packages change often, so check prices at the gate. Weekdays are far less crowded.

bayazid-bostami-shrine.desc: This shrine in the north of the city is dedicated to the Persian Sufi saint Bayazid Bostami, and draws a steady flow of visitors. Below the shrine is a large pond that is home to black softshell turtles, a species that is almost extinct in the wild. Pilgrims buy bread and bananas to feed them, and the turtles surface lazily to take the offerings. It is a calm, devotional place with a long history in Chattogram's spiritual life.
blocks: How to get there
In the Bayazid area of the city, easy to reach by CNG or ride-share.
Good to know
Dress modestly. Feed the turtles only with what is sold for that purpose.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
baroiyadhala-national-park.desc: Baroiyadhala was declared a national park on 6 April 2010 and covers about 2,934 hectares of hill forest in Sitakunda upazila. It is an important corridor for wildlife that is disappearing elsewhere, including the mainland serow, barking deer, marbled cat, macaques, pangolin and kalij pheasant. Most visitors come for the streams: rocky jhiri paths lead up to waterfalls, and the Khoiyachora falls lie within the park's forest. Away from those trails it is quiet, green and little visited.
blocks: How to get there
Take a Dhaka–Chattogram highway bus to Sitakunda, then a CNG to the Baroiyadhala area and hire a local guide there for the trails.
Good to know
Go with a local guide; trails are not marked. Wear shoes with grip, as rocks in the streams are slippery. Do not climb wet rock faces, and turn back if heavy rain makes the water rise.

glance: Gani Bakery in Chandanpura, Chattogram city, and bakeries across the old town
chattogram-bela-biscuit.desc: Bela biscuit is Chattogram's own tea-time biscuit: round, dry and crisp, and it softens nicely when dipped in milk tea. Gani Bakery in Chandanpura, founded by Abdul Gani Showdagar in the 1880s, is credited with starting it and still bakes it today. Locals buy it by the packet to take home as a gift from the port city.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
Small entry ticket; boat and kayak hire extra
mohamaya-lake.desc: Mohamaya Lake in Durgapur union of Mirsharai was created around 2009–2010 by damming the Mohamaya stream for irrigation. It is often called the country's second largest man-made lake after Kaptai, and it winds for kilometres between forested hills. Visitors hire boats or kayaks to paddle up the narrow arms of the lake, and a small waterfall feeds it at the far end. It makes an easy day trip from Chattogram, often combined with the Mirsharai waterfalls.
blocks: How to get there
Take a Dhaka-bound bus from Chattogram (Oxygen or AK Khan) and get off at Thakurdighi, Mirsharai; a CNG or rickshaw takes you to the lake gate.
Good to know
Wear a life jacket on kayaks. Weekdays are far less crowded.

glance: About 250–400 BDT per plate at restaurants
Mezban-style restaurants around GEC and Jamal Khan in Chattogram city
mezban.desc: Mezban is both a dish and an event. Families host these feasts to mark a death anniversary, a celebration or a blessing, and invite anyone who comes. Huge pots of beef are cooked with a local spice blend until dark and glossy, served with plain rice and a thin lentil soup made with beef bones. Several restaurants in the city now serve mezban-style beef every day, so travellers can taste it without an invitation.

glance: 250 km to Chattogram by road, 6–8 hours by bus or car
sitakunda-eco-park.desc: The eco park covers forested hills on the Chandranath range in Sitakunda. A paved road winds up past a botanical garden to viewpoints looking over the Bay of Bengal and the Sandwip channel on clear days. Trails lead down to waterfalls such as Suptadhara and Sahasradhara, which are at their best in the rainy season. It is an easy nature trip from Chattogram and pairs well with Chandranath Hill.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus from Chattogram toward Sitakunda and get off at the eco park gate on the Dhaka–Chattogram highway; walk or take a CNG up the hill.
Good to know
The waterfall trails are slippery in monsoon; wear good shoes and do not go alone after dark.
